source: ACIAR / University of New England / CARE, "IPM Field Guide for Soybean Pest Management in Cambodia," ACIAR project field guide, 2006
text:
This ACIAR/University of New England/CARE field guide is built specifically around Integrated Pest Management (IPM) for soybean in Cambodia. It teaches farmers a systematic field-scouting method: walk the field in a set pattern (e.g. a zig-zag or W-shaped transect), sample a fixed number of plants or a fixed row length at several points, and count pests and defoliation levels rather than treating on a calendar or on sight of a single insect.

Growth stages are referenced using the standard soybean staging system, vegetative stages VE–V6+ (VE = emergence, VC = cotyledon, V1, V3, V5... counting to the nth trifoliate leaf) and reproductive stages R1–R8 (R1 = beginning bloom, R2 = full bloom, R3 = beginning pod, R4 = full pod, R5 = beginning seed, R6 = full seed, R7 = beginning maturity, R8 = full maturity), because pest damage thresholds and yield sensitivity change through these stages.

A defoliation-percentage reference chart (5%, 15%, 35%, 45% leaf area lost, illustrated with sample leaf silhouettes) is used to standardize how much leaf damage farmers are actually looking at before deciding to act — the guide notes soybean can tolerate meaningful defoliation (cited around up to 35% before bloom, and less once seed-fill has started) without significant yield loss, which is the core IPM argument against reflexive spraying.

Numeric guidance is given for converting a sweep-net insect count or a beat-sheet count per unit row length or per square meter into an estimated insect density per square meter, with worked example tables (e.g. relating sweep counts of 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 per sweep to counts per m² by crop growth stage, before and after flowering) so farmers can compare their count against a published economic threshold rather than guess.
